newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Telstra excludes telephony from Internet package.
newsitem.headline: Telstra excludes telephony from Internet package.

text.p: Australian telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp on Monday launched its broad-band Internet access service but said the package would exclude telephony.
Telstra Multimedia chief executive Gerry Moriarty, speaking at the launch of its "Big Pond" service in Melbourne, denied the state-owned company was trying to protect its narrow-band phone network.
"It (telephony) would cause security problems for the users of the service and it would cause performance problems. That's not what we want," Moriarty said.

"Telephony is something we are studying ... If we do (go ahead with it), we will do so in a way that's based on confidence in the technology and an understanding of all the implications...," he added.
The "Big Pond" service is available to a potential market of about one million homes in Sydney and Melbourne, in areas where Telstra's optic-fibre network has been rolled out, Telstra said.
The service is many times times faster than Telstra's Internet access over the copper-wire, narrow-band network, but will be billed on the basis of volume rather than time.
Telstra expects Internet users to pay, on average, between A$80 and A$100 per month to use the "Big Pond" service, or about the same cost for those now using the narrow band network.
But, Moriarty said, "Big Pond" offered blazing speed.
In a demonstration, Telstra's general manager for broadband product development, Philip Sykes, drew gasps from Internet users by downloading a 10 megabyte file in seconds.
The same task could take over 30 minutes on the narrow-band network, Telstra said.
The "Big Pond" product is the second major product to be offered on Telstra's optic-fibre cable network.
The first was its Foxtel pay-television joint venture with The News Corp Ltd.
